chunks: A number of our companions, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Khālid, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from the one who mentioned it, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:

An affluent man came to Rasūl Allāh صلى الله عليه وآله wearing clean clothes, and he sat near Rasūl Allāh صلى الله عليه وآله. Then a poor man wearing dirty clothes came and sat beside the affluent man, so the affluent man gathered up his clothes from beneath his thighs. Rasūl Allāh صلى الله عليه وآله said to him: “Did you fear that something from his poverty might touch you?” He said, “No.” He said: “Then did you fear that something from your wealth might reach him?” He said, “No.” He said: “Then did you fear that he might soil your clothes?” He said, “No.”

He said: “Then what made you do what you did?” He said: “O Rasūl Allāh, I have a companion who makes every ugly thing seem fair to me and makes every good thing seem ugly to me, and I have given him half of my wealth.” Then Rasūl Allāh صلى الله عليه وآله said to the poor man: “Will you accept?” He said: “No.” The man said to him: “Why not?” He said: “I fear that what entered into you may enter into me.”

key_terms.فَقْرِهِ: his poverty or state of need
key_terms.قَرِينًا: an accompanying influence or inner associate that affects one's behavior
key_terms.مُعْسِرٌ: a poor or financially constrained person
key_terms.يُزَيِّنُ: makes something appear attractive or appealing
key_terms.يُقَبِّحُ: makes something appear ugly or blameworthy

ai.seo_question: What does this hadith teach about how wealthy Muslims should treat the poor?
ai.summary: This hadith teaches humility, dignity, and proper conduct toward the poor. It condemns arrogance based on wealth and shows that moral corruption can arise from inner impulses that beautify evil and distort good.
